To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

ANIT-induced reversible cholestasis leads in mice to a decreased seizure susceptibility which can be modulated by opioidergic and nitric oxide pathway, and is reversible even after the resolution of the liver disease.

ANIT-induced reversible cholestasis leads, in a time-dependent manner, to an increased resistance to PTZE-induced seizures through an NO- and opioidergic system-mediated pathway, and that this increased seizure resistance is associated with a downregulation in the opioidergic tone, which is reversed after the resolution of the cholestasis.
cholestasis induced by ANIT leads to a reversible increase in seizure threshold through opioidergic and NO pathways.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of a reversible cholestasis model on the susceptibility to seizures.
the effects of cholestasis on seizure susceptibility and the mechanisms involved.
the effects of liver cholestasis on the central nervous system and its modulation by opioidergic and nitric oxide pathways.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

ANIT-induced reversible cholestasis leads, at a certain stage of the disease, to a significant decrease in seizure susceptibility, which is likely to be mediated by opioidergic and NO signaling pathways.
ANIT-induced reversible cholestasis results in increased seizure threshold through an opioid/ NO-mediated pathway.
cholestatic liver disease may have a significant impact on the central nervous system, with a possible role in the development of neurological complications in cholestasis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

cholestasis leads, in the brain, to an increased resistance to seizures, which is mediated by an opioid/NO signaling pathway, and that opioid receptor down-regulation is a possible mechanism for this resistance.
the cholestatic state is associated with a decrease in susceptibility to seizures and that this is mediated, at least in part, by an increase in opioidergic tone and NO signaling.
the cholestasis-induced increased seizure susceptibility is mediated by opioidergic and NO signaling pathways.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the opioid/NO-mediated mechanism is not a permanent change in the brain and that the cholestatic-induced changes in seizure susceptibility can be reversed.
the central nervous effects of cholestasis are not limited to the period of disease but may also extend after the resolution of the cholestatic condition.
cholestasis can alter seizure susceptibility and the opioidergic and NO pathway are involved in the modulation of seizure susceptibility in a reversible cholestasis model.
